the_ruling_verbatim: So I have an observation that this would be a good time to discuss before we move on. the history creates noise. opus will see a thing as true because of an outdated bit of history... because even beyond me trying to keep history he does too. More information than I would. my first thought was: intention based programming means we NEVER do something part way. like a migration. because then we have multiple states in the system. now that doesn't mean we should never migrate something slowly, but it should be the exception not the rule. in the same vein, once history is done enough, maybe we move it out. or summarize it. have summarizing passes periodically? i dunno. so I'm asking: how should we handle this?
and i only added slash ruled to be emphatic that yes, this is a big pass, but worth the trouble, so ruled, approved, ticket and sail, go go go, lgtm, etc. etc.
now_the_spec_says: Every artifact is one tense: present-tense rewrites to read as written today, provenance as ticket ids; past-tense is append-only, loaded only via a compiled current-truth face. Summarizing rides PROVED. A migration is atomic unless a ticket cursor owns the partway.
the_reason_that_dies: No file dies — what dies is a style and an approach, both to be swept by the children. The dated-append house style dies: it felt like Law 7 discipline (never lose the story), but Law 7 governs records of truth and a charter is not one — it is the settled design, and git keeps its every prior version; appending history into it makes the file every mind reads first accrete stale claims a model reader weights as current truth, the exact noise the observation names. Periodic summarizing passes die too, for the standing reason polls die here: the event already fires (the PROVED crossing), and a clock re-reading everything is the daemon-reflex this corpus has corrected before. The dated-append specimens on disk (ground_loop's charter among them) die by rewrite in child the-present-tense-corpus-rewrites-once.
